headline: Approved Families in Transition loan consolidation (12-2), Aged and Infirmed Shelter funding transfers, and Tirrell House lease termination; tabled $20.8 million DPW bond.
summary: During public comment, residents raised concerns about homelessness, policing and the Nickenley Turenne police shooting, parking, e-bikes, and school enrollment versus spending. The board approved a large consent agenda, funding transfers for the Aged and Infirmed Shelter and opioid-response programs, a Families in Transition loan consolidation, new police parking and other staff positions, traffic regulation changes, and a community mural at Cullerot Park, while tabling a North Church Street discontinuance petition, a $20,800,000 DPW bond, and giving direction on Tax Collector evening hours starting November 10.
decisions: Voted to take all public comments under advisement and receive and file any written documentation presented.
Approved the Consent Agenda, covering items 2-14 and 16-27.
Approved the Families in Transition request to consolidate four loans, 12-2 roll call with Kantor and Sapienza voting nay.
Approved extending the deadline of CIP 210623 Public Health Preparedness to December 31, 2027.
Accepted the Manchester School District Priority I status and financial report submitted by LeftField for the period ending July 2026.
Accepted with regret the resignation of Thomas Hickman as a Resident Commissioner of the Manchester Housing and Redevelopment Authority.
Accepted with regret the resignation of Richard Clegg from the Housing Commission.
Accepted with regret the resignation of Shannon Sullivan from the Arts Commission.
Nominations of Suzanne Riel (Arts Commission) and Christine Leary (Housing and Redevelopment Authority) will layover until the next meeting.
Confirmed Gary Turgiss as Residential Assessor after suspending the rules.
Approved the nomination of Jane Beaulieu as Manchester's representative on the Piscataquog River Local Advisory Committee.
Approved sending written notice to the State of New Hampshire to terminate the use-of-premises agreement for the Tirrell House at 15 Brook Street.
Approved Aged and Infirmed Shelter funding transfers ($110,952.72 from Revo Casino, $50,000 opioid abatement funds) and the rent contract through October 2027, Kantor and Sapienza opposed.
Approved authorizing department heads to apply directly for grants with no City-match requirement without prior board approval.
Approved $110,592.72 for CIP C160060227 Aged and Infirmed Shelter Project, Kantor and Sapienza opposed.
Approved transfers of $120,000, $50,000, $45,000, and $66,500 among CIP accounts for shelter, café, fire Squad 1, and CRU programs, Kantor and Sapienza opposed.
Approved $25,000 transfer for the City's Special Event Reserve Account (Roll Off Containers for Drop Off).
Approved $1,100 transfer for CIP 712622 ARPA - Revenue Replacement - Roads & Sidewalks.
Approved $68,900 transfer for CIP 611423 ARPA - Homelessness Response & Emergency Shelter Operations, Kantor and Sapienza opposed.
Approved $106,395.33 for CIP 211723 Opioid Litigation Settlement Trust.
Enrolled multiple Finance Committee resolutions covering CIP amendments for roundabout, grant, dental, and other programs.
Approved the amended bylaws for the Manchester Development Corporation.
Approved a community mural for the press box at Cullerot Park.
Approved adding two full-time Parking Control Officer positions to the Parking Division.
Approved creating one full-time Payroll Administrator II position, grade 117, and ordained the corresponding ordinance.
Approved modifying the Benefits Manager position from grade 118 to grade 119 and updating its class specification.
Approved creating two Accountant II positions and eliminating two Accountant I positions in the Aviation Department.
Approved new parking regulations on Elm Street and Chestnut Street near Hanover Street.
Enrolled four Resolutions amending FY2024-FY2027 Community Improvement Program funds for roundabout, highway safety, ACERT, and dental programs.
Enrolled a Bond Resolution authorizing $27,000 for the 2026 CIP C330040426 Women's Locker Room Expansion.
Ordained an ordinance amendment raising the Art Commission's spending authorization without board approval to $1,000 per project.
Petition to discontinue a portion of North Church Street remained tabled.
Approved the petition to discontinue the Caron Street turn-around.
Received and filed the Tax Collector office hours report, with plans to start Tuesday evening hours until 8 p.m. on November 10.
Bond Resolution authorizing $20,800,000 for the 2027 CIP C500070327 Raise - City Funds (DPW-Highway) remained tabled.

BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
September 1, 2026 at 7:00 PM 
 
Mayor Ruais called the meeting to order.   
 
Mayor Ruais called for the Pledge of Allegiance; this function being led by Alderman 
Sapienza. 
  
 
A moment of silence was observed.   
 
The Clerk called the roll. 
 
Present: Aldermen Kaw-uh, Goonan, Dexter, Fajardo, Bonilla, Kantor, Trisciani, 
  O’Neil, Terrio, Sapienza, Burkush, Barry, Vincent, Thomas 
 
Mayor Ruais: I have two proclamations for this evening. Would Miss Karen Sutkus please 
come forward?  City of Manchester, a Resolution: Whereas Karen S utkus has been 
serving as the city's healthy aging specialist with the Manchester Health Department since 
August of 2023, providing critically needed assistance to older residents to ensure they 
are able to live and age safely in their homes. And whereas K aren has demonstrated 
exceptional dedication to serving Manchester's older residents by helping them navigate 
complex challenges with compassion, professionalism and unwavering commitment. And 
whereas, through collaboration with city officials, city depart ments, agencies and 
community partners, Karen has helped more than 300 older residents, supporting them 
in their homes and connecting them to resources and essential services to optimize their 
health and safety and maintain their independence. And whereas Karen has also helped 
residents through critical housing transitions, including most recently, ward three 
Selectman Glenn Ouellette, by connecting him with resources, guidance and temporary 
housing while working toward a permanent solution, enabling him to remain connected to 
the community he serves and continue fulfilling his responsibilities as an elected official. 
And whereas the City of Manchester is grateful for Karen's outstanding service through 
the Manchester Health Department and her lasting impact  on the lives of countless 
residents through her compassion, leadership and commitment to public service. Now, 
therefore, I, Jay  Ruais, Mayor of the City of Manchester, do hereby recognize and 
commend Karen for her exceptional service and dedication to the residents of Manchester 
and extend my sincere appreciation for her commitment to strengthening our community 
and improving the lives of those in it. Thank you so much.
September 1, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 2 of 67 
 
PUBLIC COMMENT   
 
1. The Mayor advised that the purpose of the public comment session is to give 
residents of Manchester the opportunity to address the Board. All people wishing 
to speak must sign up with their name, address and topic. Once called, they will 
have up to three minutes to speak and any comments must be directed to the 
chair and concluded when their time is up. If the Clerk calls their name and they 
are not present to speak, they will not be given a second opportunity. Any 
resident wishing to speak will come forward to the nearest microphone, clearly 
state their name and address when recognized and give their comments. 
 
Elaine D'Allaire: I'm speaking tonight to address a severe violation of my basic civil rights 
to safety in my community. I have taken over nine months of pictures, thousands, in fact; 
the city has only a small sample. In December of 2025, the city piled 6 to 7 feet of snow 
in the only disability spot . The ramp areas were okay for the YMCA to carry on their 
business while the ADA spot was illegally breached . Trucks were over snow piles.  The 
city knows it has an ordinance which stipulates after a storm, the city is compelled to clear 
it within 24 hours. The people in charge tonight are fully aware of its codes, ordinances 
and ADA federal laws. A total breakdown of the ADA enforcement is on Stark Street. I am 
also speaking tonight about our city being less than candid to their constituents. I have 
gathered documents, voluptuous in nature, showing the mayor knows the city is in serious 
trouble by turning it over to oversight to the police de partment, the purpose solely to 
mitigate the city's liability. I am speaking tonight because after many months of 
investigations, I asked for an unbiased internal investigation by the parking manager, who 
was absent of her fiduciary duty , to acknowledge my  email. Then Miss Faye Morrison 
split duties with someone , creating a parking supervisor. He refused my investigation 
twice, and the mayor's office supported the parking department's false claim that an 
investigation was not necessary since there was more parking. Then Dana thanked the 
supervisor in an email for stopping government oversight. Dana cannot have it both ways. 
I am just pointing out the civil laws protecting disabled people, and it's not happening 
here. The YMCA is federally compelled through t itle three, a non-profit public entity and 
local governments. Title two compels the city government and the YMCA to provide public 
access. Hence the ramp ; the ADA mandates access and it's an obligation.  I'm saying 
again, legally, the city is liable for my safety and any harm or death stemming from a 
person who threatened my life. The police decided to lower my priority and it took two 
hours on 20th of August . The police decided to lower my priority because the man who
September 1, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 3 of 67 
 
accosted me said we were having a mutua l argument. The police advised I get an order 
and I did just that. The judge granted my order of protection. You need to take serious 
action against David. 
 
Lisa Gravel, Belmont Street: South side is the gift that just keeps on giving. I looked into 
Southside's enrollment numbers and what I found is upsetting. When fifth grade was 
added to Southside in the 2021-2022 school year, it had 853 students. Today it has 744. 
That's 109 fewer students. A nearly 13% decline. And yet we're spending $59.4 million  
renovating and expanding the school to accommodate 1200 students. So, I have to ask, 
what the hell is wrong with you people spending tens of millions of dollars expanding a 
school while enrollment is declining as financially indefensible? There are only t wo 
explanations. Either the people making these decisions are complete idiots, or they have 
become so comfortable being reckless with taxpayer money that price tags don't even 
matter anymore. Either possibility is equally inexcusable. There is a reason cli ps of me 
speaking at these meetings have gone viral on Facebook. It's the same reason strangers 
are stopping me on South Willow Street while I'm delivering mail just to vent. People are 
fed up. One thing I keep hearing is Mayor Gravel, which blows my mind. I am not saying 
this to toot my horn. I am merely a canary in the coal mine. People are angry, they are 
frustrated, and they are desperate for somebody , anybody in this city government , who 
actually gives a damn about what it is costing ordinary people to live here. Every taxpayer 
in this city needs to understand the aldermen that voted to override the tax cap don't care 
about you, especially miss wannabe mayor, who is already promising she intends to 
override the tax cap again next year. To them, we are n othing but a cash cow and they 
intend to milk us dry. Their answer to everything is to raise your taxes . Budgeting, 
spending within your means, apparently that is only for us peons paying the bills. Luckily 
for this board at the moment, I have no intention  of running for public office. But who 
knows, they may just force me into it. And if they thought Joe Kelly Levasseur was a pain 
in the ass, they ain't seen nothing yet. To those of you that have reached out, thank you, 
but you need to make your voices hea rd too. Trust me, I would rather be having a root 
canal than taking time out of my life to come speak to these a -holes. But they need to 
hear it. Your silence makes it easy for them to ignore you. We need to fill their voicemails, 
flood their inboxes, and especially fill the aldermanic hall. But you don't have to wait for a 
meeting. If you run into them around town, tell them exactly how you feel, even if it is only
September 1, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 4 of 67 
 
a ditto what Gravel said. Trust me, they will know what you mean. I hope to see some of 
you here next month. Come on in. The water is warm. 
 
Kathleen Carswell, Ward 4: I've been in the city for 64 years, and I got two issues tonight. 
The first one is, can we do something about the e -bikes? I almost took out a person on 
an e-bike the other day because he cut right out from an alley on an e-bike, zipping past 
me down. I almost had a heart attack  because they're driving crazy. They're on the 
sidewalks going the wrong way. They're going faster than my car. They can go up to 30, 
35 miles an hour, if not faster. Can we please do something about regulating that? To get 
that in order would be greatly appreciated because I know I'm not the only one. The 
second issue is the sex offenders in Manchester. Do you realize we have over 500 sex 
offenders living in Manchester alone now in our state? So now we got the big prize for the 
state. Everyone's coming here. Vermont. They're coming here. Massachusetts is coming 
here. Tennessee. They're coming here. They're coming from everywhere because they 
hide in another state so they don't get caught. They don't have to register. But we have a 
lot of homeless ones. How is this city being safe compared to that? It's not. We have 
children going to school that got to walk over a mile before they can even get a bus if 
they're allowed to get a bus. And we got them. I have a new one that just moved in across 
the street from me. I'm not letting that one go. I went to go see where the landlord was. I 
know where she lives. I'm going to go talk to her. I've already talked to her. A couple of 
businesses, they fired people because they didn't realize they were sex offenders. One 
was a greeter at a diner ; a greeter. Disgusting. If you read his article, you'd be throwing 
up in your bowels right now. How many of you, raise your hand if you've been abused or 
sexually violated when you were a child? It's disgusting. And it's got to stop. I need help. 
I called the Governor's office. They told me to go to the Senate. I tried calling people in 
the Senate. No one returns my calls. I try people here. No one returns my calls. What are 
we going to do? Can we please band together to get this under control when you have 
over 500 and that outnumbers the homeless? That's disgusting. It's bad enough we have 
the homeless problem that we can't addre ss and get straightened out. Now we got sex 
offenders and you got 18 of them living right down a half a block from you, right here in a 
rooming house and across the street is Families in Transition. You got another one living 
in the shelter on Manchester Street. You know, it's disgusting and it's got to stop. We got 
to get this under control. And I'm going to come back here every time if I have to.
September 1, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 5 of 67 
 
 
Troy Micklon, 29 Ode Way: Tonight's agenda contains several items involving 
homelessness and the growing cost s of Manchester taxpayers. First, I support the 
committee's recommendation to receive and file Families in Transition’s request for an 
additional $2.5 million. I do, however, have concerns regarding their request to 
consolidate multiple city backed loans, regardless of the organization's mission. Why is 
Manchester functioning as a bank providing million dollar, zero interest financing in the 
first place? The city already borrows millions itself through bonding. If we can't pay our 
own bills, we shouldn't be  paying for somebody else's ; money isn't my only concern. 
Public funding should come with accountability, oversight and public safety standards. 
Recently, needles were reportedly found in and around a property on Amherst Street. 
Then, this last weekend, attention was brought to 15 registered sex offenders staying at 
Manchester Street Shelter. I verified those for the state registry and also found one person 
listing the 200 Elm Street shelter. If the city is funding even a single dollar, directly or 
indirectly, we should know who is using these facilities, where they're coming from and 
what safeguards are in place to protect them and our surrounding community. We should 
also be tracking whether people are seeking services, come from other communities, and 
making sure that Manchester taxpayers aren't picking up the bills for those. New 
Hampshire law provides a mechanism, under certain circumstances, for recovering those 
costs from another city or town. Are we actually using any of those provisions? And if so, 
how much has the city recovered to this date? I bring this up because Goffstown officials 
recently described problems with homelessness, homeless encampments, needles and 
theft concerns in their community, and are considering stronger ordinances and 
enforcement as surrounding communities crack down. Manchester cannot continue to be 
the destination for everyone they push out. We should help people that are in genuine 
need, especially our own residents. But Manchester taxpayers should not be expected to 
continue carrying the homelessness burden for the entire region. Compassion requires 
accountability. Protect our taxpayers, protect our public safety, and stop making 
Manchester a magnet. 
 
Patrick Binder, 96 Allen Street: I'm here tonight to talk about lawlessne ss. You know, I 
drive downtown just to come to this meeting, and I see lawlessness everywhere. Last 
time I was here , I was speaking about the parking. I saw ten cars illegally parked just
September 1, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 6 of 67 
 
outside. I spoke to a police officer about it and it's like he didn' t even see them. 
Lawlessness. You go by the park and there's drug deals in the open. I've talked to those 
people and they say that they are allowed to do drug deals there. That's lawlessness. You 
see these totally drugged out people standing on the corner, just completely drugged out. 
Lawlessness, and this body refusing to let MPD work with federal law enforcement , 
lawlessness. We had an article in the news where another city let a guy go, and then he 
was picked up by federal law enforcement. He was wanted for murder in Brazil. We don't 
want that happening here on our streets. It's lawlessness. And what is this lawlessness  
going to lead to? It just leads to more crime. What have we seen recently? Stabbing on 
the rail trail. Dozens of cars broken into on the west side. I've had my own car broken into 
over there. Windows smashed in. When you have this lawlessness, it's going to lead to 
more crime. This has been well studied. We are making a city that looks like a place  
where criminals can thrive. And they will.  And this body, I don't really trust it not to just 
vote for more lawlessness. So, I hope you guys change your ways and start voting to 
crack down on crime. Start empowering MPD to do more and to work with federal law 
enforcement.  
 
Jennifer Narby, 398 Not re Dame Avenue: Lawlessness is a nice way to start this. I live 
on the west side, and there have been vandalisms by juveniles that you guys are afraid 
of. They have had video witness reports. You knew who they were a month ago and it's 
under investigation. I want to know where these kids are. What did you do? And why is it 
still happening? Because I still have neighbors telling me that their cars are being broken 
into and windows smashed . We're afraid of these children ? Your secretary told me her 
own grandmother’s car got broken into. I don't know if she told you about it. I was looking 
out my window and there was a police officer on the street because another person on 
Notre Dame on their street got broken into. Do you know what the cops said to me? Can 
you do me a favor? He wanted me to do him a favor. Nice guy. Even good looking. 
Because that's important. He wanted me to find out if one of the cameras that we had on 
our house, which isn't even our house, we rent it, had a video. More video. We did give it 
to the police department. Not that they needed any more, but I said, you have a lot of 
nerve asking me for a favor. What are you doing about it? Do you know he was out there 
for ten minutes? He was out there for a while talking to people. Do you know what he said 
more than anything? I don't know. So that's what we got a lot of: I don't knows. Now, I am
September 1, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 7 of 67 
 
not from Manchester originally. I've lived here for 14 years with my husband and 14 years 
ago it was a lot different. It is being overrun. I don't know whether it's fear, racism, bullshit, 
but it's ridiculous. There were so many people that I reached out to just to try to get to 
come down here. This is the last thing I want to be doing is be here. Do you know what 
most of the people said after they said they'd be here, but they're not ? Why bother? 
Nothing ever gets done. I'll be back. 
 
Dave Narby, 398 Notre Dame Avenue: This is in relation to all the break ins that 
happened, which have been going on for at least six weeks, probably two months. I am 
personally aware of over $3,000 in damage from people I personally know that happened. 
They found out who did this. They pretty much wrapped it up in a bow and gave it to the 
MPD, and still it went on for weeks. I mean, there must  have been dozens of thousands 
of dollars in damage. Is there a limit that has to be reached like $25,000 before something 
gets done? And also, I have a question for you. It's been brought to my attention that you 
will not instruct MPD to work with ICE to get rid of criminal, illegal aliens in our community. 
Is that true? 
 
Mayor Ruais: No. 
 
D. Narby: It's not. So, you have instructed them to cooperate with ICE? 
 
Mayor Ruais: They regularly work with ICE. 
 
D. Narby: Have you been instructed to cooperate with ICE? My understanding is that they 
just see if there's a warrant for them locally. They don't check with the FBI. They don't 
check if there's national warrant. They don't check if there's an Interpol warrant. Because 
a lot of these criminal aliens have Interpol warrants. I mean, how bad does it have to get? 
Do more people have to get stabbed? Does somebody have to get shot? I mean, how 
bad do things have to get before something actually gets done? 
 
Audience Member: They're not criminals, sir. 
 
D. Narby: We can talk outside if you want.
September 1, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 8 of 67 
 
 
Mayor Ruais: Relax; let's keep it civil, please. 
 
D. Narby: We've been relaxed up to this point and it's gotten us to where? Who knows 
how many thousands in damage? When does it stop? When does it stop? Figure it out. 
 
Brittany Ping, 199 Putnam Street: I wear a lot of hats. And today I am bringing troop leader 
of Girl Scout Troop 63333. It's a lot of threes. We are based in a homeschooling co-op in 
Derry, New Hampshire, but our members come from all around the state of N ew 
Hampshire. Obviously, I'm a troop leader. My daughter in West Manchester is part of it. I 
lead our cadets in the troop or a multi-age troop that's sixth, seventh and eighth graders. 
I also work with a nonprofit called We Heart West. I'm one of the found ers and we have 
the unique privilege of managing the play ball community garden at Cullerot Park, which 
is at Northwest Elementary. It was a t -ball park. Manchester Grows worked with the city 
of Manchester to turn it into a beautiful community garden. We'v e been very blessed at 
We Heart West to receive a grant. We were able to expand our community gardens. I 
brought our Girl Scout troop there because I was hoping they could help. We Heart West 
host a community event, and two of our cadets looked at this pre ss box and they said, 
what are you doing with that? And I said, we really want to do a community mural. And 
they said a community mural , could we do it? I said, yes; girl led activities , this is what 
we're about. What would you want to do? I need you to create this mural. I need you to 
come up with a design  and we want it to be community focused. We want people who 
come, people who plant in those garden beds, if you have not come by, please come by. 
It's beautiful. I went and took pictures today to show y ou what the press box looks like 
today. So, you'll see that the paint’s a little bit rough on three sides. We need to do some 
pressure washing and you'll see that it's been tagged. So, this tagging is pretty recently. 
It's within the past few months actually. So, the Girl Scouts, we started working on this in 
June and this tagging was there before our next meeting at the park in July. I have to 
admit that I kind of forgot that we have to come to you guys, because you own the press 
box. We were so excited to  try to do this in August , and then you guys did n’t meet in 
August. So, thank you so much to the Building and Lands Committee for approving this 
to come in front of the board today. I've done a quick snapshot so you can see what it 
looks like today this morning. And you can see the four-season mural that the girls have
September 1, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 9 of 67 
 
designed that they would like to be able to implement in a community mural event. And 
we would love, of course, for you to be there so you can do your fall leaf handprint on the 
back. You can  do your hand -drawn snowflake and your tulip on the front of our spring 
garden that will announce the community garden to the community when they pull in the 
parking lot. I love the city of Manchester. It's really hard sometimes, and so bright spots 
like these are why I do what I do. I know that these bright spots are why you guys do what 
you do. So, thank you so much for your time and please approve the community mural 
project.
